UNIT 12: GLACIAL PROCESSES AND LANDFORMS

KEY THEME
- Glaciers shaped the Irish landscape in three main ways: erosion (carving and wearing the landscape), transportation (moving their load downslope) and deposition (dropping their load as they melt).
- Learning outcomes: name and explain glacial erosion, transportation and deposition; identify evidence of glacial processes in landforms on the Irish landscape.

KEY TERMS
- Glaciation: the process by which land is covered by glaciers or ice sheets over long periods, shaping the landscape through erosion and deposition. Also describes how glaciers form, move, advance and retreat.
- Ice Age (glaciation): a long period of colder global temperatures when large ice sheets and glaciers cover large parts of the Earth.
- Valley glaciers: glaciers that form in mountains and flow downhill through valleys.
- Continental ice sheets: massive, thick layers of ice covering large land areas (e.g. Greenland and Antarctica today).
- Accumulation: the process by which a glacier gains mass, mainly through snowfall, freezing rain or wind-blown snow.
- Ablation: loss of ice from a glacier through melting, evaporation or calving.
- Glacier mass balance: the difference between accumulation (gain) and ablation (loss) of ice over time.
- Line of equilibrium: the boundary on a glacier where accumulation equals ablation.
- Deformation: bending or internal change in shape of glacier ice due to pressure, helping it move (similar to plastic flow).

GLACIATIONS IN IRELAND
- Ireland had two major glaciations (Ice Ages).
- The Munsterian (300,000 to 130,000 years ago): all of Ireland covered by ice up to 300 m thick; only the highest mountains stuck out, forming pyramidal peaks or nunataks.
- Nunatak: a pointed mountain sticking up out of an ice sheet, e.g. Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo.
- The Devensian/Midlandian (80,000 to 12,000 years ago): at its height all of Ireland was covered, but mainly about two-thirds was covered, with the exception of Munster. It ended about 12,000 years ago (the last Ice Age).
- Vatnajokull Glacier in Iceland is an ice cap the size of Leinster; Ireland looked like this 20,000 years ago.

HOW GLACIERS FORM
- Falling snow builds up and is compressed; air is squeezed out of the lower layers.
- Snow (about 90% air) becomes granular ice (50% air), then firn (less than 30% air, about 20-30%), then glacial ice or blue ice (about 20% air in bubbles).
- Glacial ice is blue because the oxygen has been removed.

TYPES OF GLACIERS
- Valley glaciers: form in mountains, e.g. Aletsch Glacier, Switzerland; move slowly downslope to valleys; relatively small.
- Continental ice sheets (ice caps): very large glaciers covering vast regions. Ireland was covered by these in the last Ice Age, and they shaped today's landscape. Today: Antarctica and Greenland.

GLACIER MASS BALANCE
- Snow builds up in the mountains and turns to ice. When the pile is big enough it deforms and flows downslope under its own weight and gravity, slowly (max. 25 cm per day). The area where snow and ice build up is the accumulation zone.
- Lower down, temperatures are warmer, so the glacier melts, retreats and gets smaller (ablation) in the ablation zone.
- When accumulation equals ablation, the ice will not move: this is the line of equilibrium (snow line), an important climate indicator.
- If the climate warms, the equilibrium line moves up the glacier; if it cools, the line moves down. As the global climate heats up, the equilibrium line of almost all glaciers will move up.
- Diagram (Fig 12.6): accumulation zone at top (gain, positive balance), equilibrium line, ablation zone below (loss, negative balance), direction of flow over bedrock.

GLACIER MOVEMENT
- Basal sliding: once ice reaches about 50 m deep it spreads outwards and downwards under its own weight. The base is in contact with the ground and is slightly warmer, so a thin layer of meltwater forms. This acts as a lubricant so the glacier slides; gravity moves it downhill.
- Plastic flow: ice deforms (changes shape) as it moves. Upper zone: ice is brittle and breaks to form crevasses. Lower zone (about 50 m down): ice under pressure changes shape without breaking, like toothpaste squeezed from a tube.
- Speed depends on: steepness of the slope; amount of ice accumulated; width of the valley space.
- Ice flow is slower at the base and sides due to friction with bedrock and valley sides, and fastest at the centre (and surface) where there is less friction.

PROCESSES OF GLACIAL EROSION
- Plucking (quarrying): the weight of ice creates pressure and friction, melting ice at the base. Meltwater seeps into rock joints, refreezes and expands by 9% (freeze-thaw action), weakening and loosening the rock. The glacier freezes onto splintered rocks, which stick to its base and sides and are pulled (plucked) away as it moves.
- Abrasion: jagged rocks stuck in the base and sides scrape, scour and gouge the land, like sandpaper (the sandpaper effect). Most rocks are bulldozed along. Rocks left behind have deep scratches called striations (striae).
- Glaciologists study striations to tell the direction glaciers moved in past Ice Ages.

GLACIAL TRANSPORTATION
- Supraglacial (on-glacial): material (till/drift) carried on the surface; weathered from valley sides by freeze-thaw or dropped by landslides or avalanches.
- Englacial: material inside the glacier; fell onto it and moved down, fell into a crevasse, or rose from the valley floor within the ice.
- Subglacial: material at the base; eroded by plucking or came down through the ice from the surface.

GLACIAL DEPOSITION
- A glacier deposits its load when it no longer has the energy to carry it: when temperatures rise and ice melts; when it reaches flat land, loses velocity and stops.
- Glacial deposits are unsorted and unstratified (mixed sizes, no layers): called glacial till, glacial drift or boulder clay.
- Meltwater also deposits material, sorted (fine silt and clay separated from larger rocks): this is fluvio-glacial deposition.

LANDFORMS OF GLACIAL EROSION
- Created by plucking and abrasion; these are more dominant at higher altitudes in the zone of accumulation.
- List: cirque/corrie/coom; arete; pyramidal peak/nunatak; U-shaped valley; hanging valley; truncated spur; ribbon lake/Pater-Noster lake.

CIRQUE (CORRIE, COOM)
- A bowl-shaped depression, steep on three sides with a gentle lip at the front; often holds a lake called a tarn. Called 'the birthplace of the glacier'.
- Examples: Devil's Punch Bowl, Mangerton Mountain, Co. Kerry; Coumshingaun, Comeragh Mountains, Co. Waterford.
- Processes: plucking, abrasion, freeze-thaw action, nivation, rotational slip.
- Formation: snow piles up in hollows high in the mountains and is compressed into ice. Freeze-thaw (ice expands about 9%) loosens and breaks rock into scree. This continuous freezing, thawing and breaking of rock is nivation; it widens and deepens the hollow so more snow collects.
- When the ice reaches 50 m it moves downslope, turning under its own weight in a sliding motion called rotational slip.
- Bergschrunds (gaps) form on the ice surface as it turns. Scree falls in and joins rocks plucked from the back and base of the hollow; these are used to scour and widen the hollow by abrasion.
- The glacier moves down the valley over the lip due to gravity. After the Ice Age, meltwater in the hollow forms a tarn.
- Diagram (Fig 12.14): hollow with bergschrund at back, plucking on back wall, rotational slip, crevasses, abrasion on floor, lip and terminal moraine at front.

ARETE AND PYRAMIDAL PEAK
- Arete: when two cirques form back-to-back, erosion of their back walls leaves a narrow ridge (e.g. beside the Devil's Punch Bowl, Co. Kerry).
- Pyramidal peak: where three or more cirques form on a mountain, erosion and weathering of their back walls leaves a pointed peak. Examples: Carrauntoohil, Co. Kerry; Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo.

U-SHAPED VALLEY
- A trough with steep sides and a wide flat floor, sometimes holding ribbon lakes. Also called a glaciated valley or glacial trough.
- Fjord: a drowned U-shaped valley, flooded when sea levels rose as ice melted after the Ice Age. Example: Killary Harbour, Leenane, Co. Galway.
- Examples: Doolough Valley, Co. Mayo; Glendalough, Co. Wicklow.
- Processes: plucking, abrasion, differential erosion, freeze-thaw action.
- Many were once V-shaped river valleys before temperatures fell.
- Freeze-thaw on upper slopes breaks off scree, which falls onto the glacier and between it and the valley side.
- Friction melts ice at the base; it refreezes onto bedrock, which is pulled out as the ice moves (plucking).
- Plucked rock in the base and sides scrapes and gouges the valley (abrasion), widening and deepening the sides and floor. Rocks left show striations.

TRUNCATED SPURS, RIBBON LAKES, HANGING VALLEYS
- Truncated spurs: glaciers cut through old interlocking spurs, bulldozing them; they appear as ridges coming down the valley side that end abruptly near the floor with a steep, often inverted V-shaped face.
- Ribbon lakes (Pater-Noster lakes): differential erosion on the valley floor (softer rock plucked and gouged more deeply than harder rock) forms hollows that fill with water; several lakes are often linked by streams.
- Hanging valleys: smaller tributary glaciers in old tributary river valleys could not erode as deeply as the main glacier. After the ice melted, these valleys were left hanging above the main valley floor. Streams form waterfalls, e.g. Glencar Waterfall, Co. Leitrim.
- Doolough Valley, Co. Mayo shows a U-shaped valley with hanging valleys, ribbon lakes and steep sides.

LANDFORMS OF GLACIAL DEPOSITION
- Formed when a glacier melts or reaches flat land: glacial till, moraines, drumlins, erratics.
- Glacial till/drift/boulder clay: deposited directly by ice, unsorted and unstratified.

MORAINES
- A moraine is a ridge of unsorted glacial till (rock, earth, sand and gravel deposited by ice). Examples: Doolough Valley, Co. Mayo; Glendalough, Co. Wicklow. Processes: melting, reduced velocity and moulding.
- Five types:
- Lateral moraines: along the sides of the glacier; loose material from upper slopes plus material from plucking and abrasion; deposited as the glacier melts.
- Medial moraines: down the centre where a tributary glacier joins a larger one and their lateral moraines merge. Only seen on modern glaciers as they are destroyed when ice melts; no obvious Irish examples.
- Terminal (end) moraines: at the front or snout of the glacier, marking its end point; run parallel to the ice front; in Ireland usually covered in vegetation.
- Recessional moraines: a series of terminal moraines across valley floors, formed when a retreating glacier halted, deposited, then retreated again; evidence of fluctuating temperatures.
- Ground moraines: when glaciers retreat rapidly (as at the end of the last Ice Age), material is spread evenly without ridges, forming gently rolling boulder clay plains.

DRUMLINS
- Oval or hump-backed hills of boulder clay, usually in large groups called swarms, giving 'basket of eggs topography'.
- Examples: Clew Bay, Co. Mayo; Drumlin Belt, Co. Cavan (swarm near Cootehill).
- Processes: melting, reduced velocity and moulding.
- Carrying capacity: the ability of ice to transport material.
- Formation: as the glacier reaches flatter land with lots of sediment, it slows and can no longer carry it, so it deposits. This happens if it melts in warmer temperatures, loses momentum on flat land or meets friction with underlying rocks.
- Basal meltwater saturates the sediment, so it is easily moulded by the ice flowing over it. If the glacier meets a resistant rock on the valley floor, sediment bunches up, ice flows over it and leaves a tailed hill.
- Size: up to 1 km long and 500 m wide, average height 50 m.
- Shape shows ice direction: the steep end (stoss slope) faced where the glacier came from; the gentle end (lee slope) faced away.

ERRATICS
- A rock or rocks differing in type and shape from the local parent rock; also called dropstones.
- Example: granite on Inis Mor, Aran Islands, Co. Galway.
- Processes: melting and reduced velocity; the glacier loses the ability to carry its load and drops boulders where the parent rock is different.

FLUVIO-GLACIAL LANDFORMS
- Fluvio-glaciation: meltwater from glaciers producing landforms. It happened as temperatures rose sharply at the end of the last Ice Age (12,000 years ago), releasing huge amounts of water.
- Because liquid water is the agent, material is sorted (fine silts and sands separated from rocks and boulders) and stratified into layers.

ESKER
- A long winding ridge of stratified glacial material. Example: Esker Riada, Clonmacnoise, Co. Offaly (the Galway to Dublin railway is built on a section of it).
- Processes: sorting, loss of velocity, loss of volume.
- Forms in tunnels under an ice sheet carrying huge volumes of meltwater. Tunnel exits get blocked by till, obstructing flow and causing deposition. Boulders, sand, gravel, silt and clay are laid down in layers, heaviest at the bottom.
- Eskers run parallel to the direction of ice flow and perpendicular to terminal moraines.

OUTWASH PLAIN
- A large flat or undulating area covered with fluvio-glacial meltwater deposits. Example: the Curragh, Co. Kildare (between Newbridge and Kildare Town).
- Processes: sorting, loss of velocity, loss of volume.
- Meltwater deposits its load in front of the ice, may flow through the terminal moraine and deposit beyond it. Heavier stones, gravel and sand are dropped first (shortest distance); lighter silts and clays travel further.
- Deposits can be up to 50 m thick and make good agricultural land.

GLACIAL SPILLWAY (FLUVIO-GLACIAL EROSION)
- A V-shaped valley channel cut by water flowing from a glacial meltwater lake. Example: Glen of the Downs, Co. Wicklow.
- Processes: hydraulic action, vertical erosion, abrasion.
- A pro-glacial lake forms when meltwater is trapped between the ice and an upland area. The lake rises until it overflows at the lowest point of the upland. The meltwater erodes vertically by abrasion and hydraulic action, cutting a V-shaped valley.
- Spillways are often dry today and give routes through uplands (e.g. Glen of the Downs).

APPLIED GEOGRAPHY PROJECT IDEAS
- Study areas: Glendalough, Doolough, Glencar, Glenveagh (Co. Donegal), Killarney. Use map and compass to find ice direction; measure valley width and height, drumlin height and slope, esker height and extent; sketch valley profile; analyse till or esker material; look for moraines and striations; note human interference such as quarrying; write a report.

SUMMARY
- Last Ice Age in Ireland: Devensian/Midlandian, ended about 12,000 years ago.
- Glaciers move by basal sliding and plastic flow; erode by plucking and abrasion; carry material supraglacially, englacially and subglacially; deposit when they melt, slow down or meet friction.
- Erosion landforms: cirques, aretes, pyramidal peaks, U-shaped valleys, ribbon lakes, truncated spurs, hanging valleys.
- Deposition landforms (unsorted till): moraines, drumlins, erratics.
- Fluvio-glacial: eskers and outwash plains (deposition), glacial spillways (erosion).

EXAM SKILLS
- HL Q3(b) style: examine evidence of glacial erosion in one named Irish landform. A cirque (e.g. Devil's Punch Bowl) is the best choice, with a simple labelled diagram.
- OL sample: drumlin answer: deposition on flatter land, melting, friction, resistant rock, stoss and lee slopes.

rows.prompt: What was the name of the last Ice Age in Ireland?
rows.explanation: The last glaciation was the Devensian/Midlandian (80,000 to 12,000 years ago).

rows.prompt: About how long ago did the last Ice Age in Ireland end?
rows.explanation: The Devensian/Midlandian ended approximately 12,000 years ago.

rows.prompt: What is a nunatak?
options: A lake in a glacial hollow
A ridge of sorted meltwater deposits
A gap in the ice at the back of a cirque
A pointed mountain sticking out of an ice sheet
rows.explanation: A nunatak is a pointed mountain protruding out of the ice, e.g. Croagh Patrick during the Munsterian.

rows.prompt: During the Munsterian glaciation, how thick was the ice over Ireland?
rows.explanation: In the Munsterian all of Ireland was covered by ice up to 300 m thick.

rows.prompt: What is the stage between granular ice and glacial ice called?
rows.explanation: Snow becomes granular ice (50% air), then firn (less than 30% air), then glacial (blue) ice.

rows.prompt: Why is glacial ice blue?
options: It reflects the colour of the sky
All the oxygen has been removed
rows.explanation: The chapter states glacial ice is blue because all the oxygen has been squeezed out.

rows.prompt: Which is an example of a continental ice sheet today?
rows.explanation: Continental ice sheets cover vast areas, such as Antarctica and Greenland today; Aletsch is a valley glacier.

rows.prompt: What is ablation?
options: Loss of ice by melting, evaporation or calving
Scraping of rock by a glacier
rows.explanation: Ablation is the loss of ice from a glacier; it happens in the ablation zone lower down where it is warmer.

rows.prompt: If the climate warms, what happens to a glacier's equilibrium line?
options: It stays in the same place
rows.explanation: Warming moves the equilibrium line up the glacier; cooling moves it down, so it is a useful climate indicator.

rows.prompt: What is the maximum speed of glacier movement given in the chapter?
rows.explanation: Glacier movement is slow, a maximum of 25 cm per day.

rows.prompt: In basal sliding, what acts as a lubricant under the glacier?
rows.explanation: The base is slightly warmer, so a thin layer of meltwater forms and lets the glacier slide over the ground.

rows.prompt: Plastic flow in a glacier is compared to what?
options: A ball rolling down a hill
rows.explanation: About 50 m down, ice under pressure changes shape without breaking, much like toothpaste squeezed out of a tube.

rows.prompt: Where in a glacier does ice flow fastest?
rows.explanation: Friction with bedrock and valley sides slows ice at the base and sides; there is less friction at the centre, so it flows faster there.

rows.prompt: By how much does water expand when it freezes in rock joints?
rows.explanation: Meltwater refreezes and expands by 9% in freeze-thaw action, loosening rock for plucking.

rows.prompt: Deep scratches left on rocks by glacial abrasion are called...
rows.explanation: Striations (striae) are scratch marks left by abrasion; they show the direction the ice moved.

rows.prompt: Which process is known as 'the sandpaper effect'?
rows.explanation: Abrasion is when rocks frozen into the glacier scrape and scour the land, grinding it down like sandpaper.

rows.prompt: Material carried inside a glacier is called...
rows.explanation: Englacial material is within the glacier; supraglacial is on top and subglacial is at the base.

rows.prompt: How is glacial till best described?
rows.explanation: Till (boulder clay) is deposited directly by ice and is mixed sizes with no layers: unsorted and unstratified.

rows.prompt: Which is an Irish example of a cirque?
rows.explanation: The Devil's Punch Bowl on Mangerton Mountain, Co. Kerry is a cirque; Coumshingaun is another.

rows.prompt: What is nivation?
options: Ice turning in a sliding motion
Continuous freezing, thawing and breaking of rock in a hollow
rows.explanation: Nivation is repeated freeze-thaw breaking rock into scree, which widens and deepens the hollow.

rows.prompt: What forms when two cirques erode back-to-back?
rows.explanation: Erosion of the back walls of two cirques leaves a narrow ridge called an arete; three or more make a pyramidal peak.

rows.prompt: Which is an Irish pyramidal peak?
rows.explanation: Carrauntoohil, Co. Kerry and Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo are pyramidal peaks.

rows.prompt: Killary Harbour, Co. Galway is an example of what?
rows.explanation: A fjord is a drowned U-shaped valley flooded by sea-level rise after the Ice Age; Killary Harbour is the example.

rows.prompt: Why are hanging valleys left above the main valley floor?
options: Sea levels rose and flooded them
Smaller tributary glaciers could not erode as deeply
rows.explanation: Tributary glaciers lacked the power to erode as deep as the main glacier, so their valleys were left hanging, e.g. Glencar Waterfall.

rows.prompt: Ribbon lakes on a valley floor form mainly because of...
rows.explanation: Softer rock is plucked and gouged more deeply than harder rock, making hollows that fill as ribbon (Pater-Noster) lakes.

rows.prompt: Which moraine marks the end point of a glacier at its snout?
rows.explanation: Terminal (end) moraines are found at the front or snout of the glacier and mark its furthest point.

rows.prompt: Recessional moraines are evidence of what?
options: Very rapid retreat of the ice
rows.explanation: Recessional moraines form when a retreating glacier halts, deposits, then retreats again, showing fluctuating temperatures.

rows.prompt: Drumlins in large groups are described as...
rows.explanation: Drumlin swarms give a 'basket of eggs topography', e.g. the Drumlin Belt in Co. Cavan.

rows.prompt: The steep end of a drumlin, which faced the oncoming ice, is called the...
rows.explanation: The stoss slope is the steep end facing where the glacier came from; the gentle lee slope faced away.

rows.prompt: Granite boulders on Inis Mor are an example of what?
rows.explanation: Erratics are rocks that differ from the local parent rock, dropped by melting ice.

rows.prompt: Which is an Irish example of an outwash plain?
rows.explanation: The Curragh, between Newbridge and Kildare Town, is an outwash plain of sorted meltwater deposits.

rows.prompt: A glacial spillway forms when...
options: a pro-glacial lake overflows and cuts a channel
sediment bunches up behind a rock
a tunnel under ice is blocked
rows.explanation: Meltwater trapped in a pro-glacial lake overflows the lowest point of the upland and cuts a V-shaped channel, e.g. Glen of the Downs.

rows.prompt: Briefly explain how glacier ice forms.
rows.model_answer: Falling snow builds up and is compressed, squeezing the air out of the lower layers. It first becomes granular ice, which is about 50% air, then firn, with less than 30% air. Finally it becomes glacial or blue ice, which is blue because the oxygen has been removed.

rows.prompt: Explain 'glacier mass balance' and why the line of equilibrium is a good indicator of climate change.
rows.model_answer: Glacier mass balance is the difference between accumulation (gain of ice in the upper zone) and ablation (loss of ice by melting lower down). The line of equilibrium is where the two are equal. If the climate warms the line moves up the glacier, and if it cools the line moves down, so its position shows whether the climate is warming or cooling.

rows.prompt: Name and explain the two ways glaciers move.
rows.model_answer: In basal sliding, the base of the glacier is slightly warmer so a thin layer of meltwater forms, which lubricates the ice and lets it slide downhill under gravity. In plastic flow, the ice deforms as it moves: the upper ice is brittle and cracks into crevasses, while ice about 50 m down changes shape under pressure without breaking, like toothpaste.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between plucking and abrasion.
rows.model_answer: In plucking, meltwater seeps into rock joints, refreezes and expands by 9%, loosening the rock, which freezes onto the glacier and is pulled away as it moves. In abrasion, the jagged rocks stuck in the base and sides of the glacier scrape and gouge the land like sandpaper, leaving scratches called striations.

rows.prompt: Briefly explain the difference between glacial deposition and fluvio-glacial deposition.
rows.model_answer: Glacial deposition is material dropped directly by ice when it melts or slows down; it is unsorted and unstratified and is called till or boulder clay. Fluvio-glacial deposition is material dropped by meltwater, so it is sorted into different sizes and stratified into layers, as in eskers and outwash plains.

rows.prompt: Name and describe three types of moraine.
rows.model_answer: Lateral moraines are ridges along the sides of a glacier made of material from the valley slopes. Terminal moraines form at the snout and mark the furthest point the glacier reached. Recessional moraines are a series of terminal moraines across the valley floor, left when a retreating glacier halted several times.

rows.prompt: Explain how an esker is formed, naming an Irish example.
rows.model_answer: Eskers form in tunnels under an ice sheet where huge volumes of meltwater carry glacial material. When the tunnel exits become blocked by till, the flow is obstructed and the water deposits boulders, sand, gravel, silt and clay in layers, with the heaviest at the bottom. The result is a long winding ridge running parallel to the ice flow, such as the Esker Riada at Clonmacnoise, Co. Offaly.

rows.prompt: What is a truncated spur and how is it formed?
rows.model_answer: A truncated spur is a ridge running down the side of a glaciated valley that ends abruptly near the valley floor with a steep, often inverted V-shaped face. It forms when a glacier, through its sheer weight and power, cuts through the old interlocking spurs of a river valley and bulldozes them out of the way.

rows.prompt: In relation to one named landform that you studied, examine evidence of glacial processes of erosion that have shaped the Irish landscape. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: A cirque is a bowl-shaped hollow, steep on three sides with a gentle lip at the front, often holding a lake called a tarn; an example is the Devil's Punch Bowl, Mangerton Mountain, Co. Kerry. Snow piled up in hollows high in the mountains and was compressed into ice. Freeze-thaw action, where water expands by about 9% when it freezes, broke rock into scree. This continuous freezing, thawing and breaking of rock is nivation, which widened and deepened the hollow so more snow gathered. When the ice reached about 50 m thick, it moved downslope, turning under its own weight in rotational slip. Gaps called bergschrunds opened at the back as it turned. Scree fell into them and joined rock plucked from the back wall and floor, as meltwater froze into joints and the ice pulled the loosened rock away. These rocks were used to scour the hollow by abrasion, deepening it and leaving striations. The glacier then spilled over the lip into the valley. After the Ice Age, meltwater filled the hollow to form a tarn. Where two cirques formed back-to-back, an arete was left between them, as at the Devil's Punch Bowl. Diagram: cross-section of hollow with bergschrund, freeze-thaw on back wall, plucking, rotational slip, abrasion on floor, lip and tarn.
rows.marking_scheme: Named landform 2m. Named Irish example 2m. Labelled diagram 4m (or credited within SRPs). Examination: 11 SRPs x 2m = 22m (e.g. snow accumulates in hollow; compressed to ice; freeze-thaw 9% expansion; scree; nivation widens hollow; 50 m ice moves; rotational slip; bergschrund; plucking explained; abrasion explained; striations; glacier over lip; tarn forms; arete from back-to-back cirques). Maximum 30m.

rows.prompt: Examine, with the aid of a labelled diagram, how glacial processes formed a U-shaped valley that you have studied. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: A U-shaped valley is a glacial trough with steep sides and a wide, flat floor, for example Doolough Valley, Co. Mayo or Glendalough, Co. Wicklow. Many were V-shaped river valleys before temperatures fell in the Ice Age. Freeze-thaw on the upper slopes broke off scree, which fell onto the glacier and between it and the valley side. Friction at the base melted the ice; the meltwater refroze onto the bedrock, and as the ice moved, rock was pulled out in plucking. The plucked rock frozen into the base and sides scraped and gouged the valley in abrasion, the sandpaper effect, widening and deepening the sides and floor and leaving striations. The glacier's weight and power cut through interlocking spurs, leaving truncated spurs that end abruptly near the floor. Differential erosion gouged softer rock more deeply, forming hollows filled by ribbon lakes, often linked by streams, as in Doolough. Smaller tributary glaciers could not erode as deeply, leaving hanging valleys with waterfalls such as Glencar, Co. Leitrim. Where sea level rose after the ice melted, the valley was drowned to form a fjord, such as Killary Harbour. Diagram: U-shaped cross-section with steep sides, flat floor, ribbon lake, truncated spur and hanging valley.
rows.marking_scheme: Named example 2m. Labelled diagram 4m. Examination: 12 SRPs x 2m = 24m (e.g. originally V-shaped; freeze-thaw/scree; basal melting and refreezing; plucking; abrasion/sandpaper; widened and deepened; striations; truncated spurs; differential erosion; ribbon lakes; hanging valleys; waterfall example; fjord/sea-level rise). Maximum 30m.

rows.prompt: Describe and explain, with the aid of a labelled diagram, the formation of one landform of glacial deposition. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: A drumlin is an oval-shaped or hump-backed hill of boulder clay, usually in swarms giving a basket of eggs topography, e.g. Clew Bay, Co. Mayo or the Drumlin Belt in Co. Cavan. As the glacier reached flatter land, it carried lots of sediment. It slowed down and its carrying capacity fell, so deposition occurred. This happened as it melted in warmer temperatures, lost momentum on flat land or met friction with underlying rocks. Meltwater at the base saturated the sediment, so it was easily moulded by the ice flowing over it. Where the glacier met a resistant rock, the sediment bunched up and the ice flowed over and continued, leaving a tailed hill. Drumlins can be up to 1 km long, 500 m wide and average 50 m high. The steep stoss slope faced the oncoming ice and the gentle lee slope faced away, showing the direction of ice flow. Diagram: cross-section and plan of a drumlin showing stoss slope, lee slope and direction of ice flow.
rows.marking_scheme: Named landform and example 2m. Labelled diagram 4m. Explanation: 7 SRPs x 2m = 14m (e.g. boulder clay; flat land/slows; carrying capacity reduced; melting/friction; saturated sediment moulded; resistant rock; ice flows over; size figures; stoss and lee slopes; shows ice direction; swarms). Maximum 20m.

rows.prompt: Describe and explain, using an Irish example, how one fluvio-glacial feature was formed. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: An outwash plain is a large flat or undulating area covered with fluvio-glacial meltwater deposits, for example the Curragh, Co. Kildare. Fluvio-glaciation happened when temperatures rose sharply at the end of the last Ice Age about 12,000 years ago, releasing huge quantities of meltwater. Because water, not ice, was the agent, the material was sorted and stratified into layers. Meltwater flowing from the ice sheet deposited its load in front of the ice. It often flowed through the terminal moraine, removing material and carrying it beyond. As the water lost velocity and volume, it deposited its load. The heaviest stones, gravel and sand were dropped first, closest to the ice, while lighter silts and clays were carried further before being deposited. These deposits can be up to 50 m thick and make good agricultural land, as at the Curragh. Diagram: ice sheet, terminal moraine, meltwater streams and outwash plain with coarse material near the ice and fine material further away.
rows.marking_scheme: Named feature and Irish example 2m. Diagram 4m. Explanation: 7 SRPs x 2m = 14m (e.g. end of Ice Age 12,000 years ago; huge meltwater; sorted; stratified; deposited in front of ice; through terminal moraine; loss of velocity/volume; heavy material first; fine material further; up to 50 m thick; good farmland). Maximum 20m.
